4 Free-choice Assignment: LabPrepMapper 4.1 Choosing a New Data Science for Biology Skill For my free-choice assignment, I would like to learn Python programming and explore the development of AI agents for laboratory settings. For this, I plan to use LangChain and Ollama. As a Life Sciences student training to become a biomedical laboratory scientist, I am interested in both molecular biology and data science. I would like to explore how these two fields can work together, as I find this combination particularly interesting. I hope to broaden my knowledge and become more versatile in this field. During Data Science for Biology 1 and 2, I have learned to program in R and Bash. However, I have always wanted to learn Python as well. With this assignment, I would like to expand my programming skills. Python interests me not only because of its applications in Life Sciences, but also because it is widely used across programming and data science. In addition, I would like to explore the development of agentic AI applications. I see a lot of potential in artificial intelligence, especially considering how quickly its use has become commonplace in society. An AI agent can do more than simply answer questions: it can also use available tools to carry out specific tasks. I would like to investigate how this could be applied in a laboratory setting. My idea is to develop my own prototype, called LabPrepMapper. This will be a locally run AI assistant that helps users prepare laboratory protocols by retrieving and organising relevant safety information about the chemicals and procedures involved. The user will provide a laboratory protocol as a PDF document, for example, exported from LabArchives. The assistant will identify the chemicals used and examine the different steps described in the protocol. Based on this information, it will look up relevant safety information in a predefined selection of reliable Safety Data Sheet (SDS) sources. This may include H-statements and P-statements, as well as relevant information about handling, personal protective equipment, first aid and waste disposal. By considering both the chemicals and the described procedures, the assistant can highlight potentially relevant safety measures that should be addressed in the protocol. I plan to run an existing language model locally using Ollama and connect it to custom Python functions through LangChain. The Python functions will handle tasks such as extracting information from the PDF and retrieving relevant SDS information. The language model will help interpret and organise the results into a structured overview. Considering my future plans, I believe this is a suitable choice. I want to develop into a biomedical laboratory scientist with both theoretical and practical knowledge of molecular biology, as well as the ability to analyse biological data. I believe that knowledge of Python and AI applications could be valuable in this field, building on the experience I already have with R and Bash. The exact chemicals, sources and functions of the assistant will be determined in consultation with my teacher. The scope and technical possibilities of the project will also be discussed before development begins. 4.2 Planning and Approach A total of 32 hours is allocated to this assignment. I aim to divide this time between learning Python and the required AI technologies, developing my own prototype and documenting the results. 4.2.1 Distribution of Available Time Activity Time Learning the basics of Python 7 hours Installing Ollama and learning to use a local model 2 hours Exploring LangChain and agentic AI 3 hours Selecting chemicals, protocol examples and reliable information sources 2 hours Developing custom Python functions 5 hours Connecting the local model to LangChain 5 hours Testing and evaluating the application 4 hours Documenting the code and results 4 hours Total 32 hours 4.2.2 Implementation Schedule I plan to spread the assignment over six weeks. This schedule takes into account the other parts of the Workflows course, the SQL assessments and the parallel Projecticum. Period Activities Time 16–22 November 2026 Installing Python and learning the basics 4 hours 23–29 November 2026 Further practising Python and selecting protocol examples and reliable sources 5 hours 30 November–6 December 2026 Installing Ollama, testing a local model and exploring LangChain 5 hours 7–13 December 2026 Developing custom Python functions for extracting protocol information and retrieving SDS data 6 hours 14–20 December 2026 Connecting the local model to LangChain and further testing 6 hours 21–27 December 2026 Testing, evaluating and documenting the application 6 hours Total 32 hours I will plan the exact working days in my calendar. This schedule is subject to discussion with and approval from my teacher. 4.3 Requirements To complete this assignment, I will need: A laptop capable of running Python and Ollama. Python and a suitable development environment. Ollama with a local language model that supports tool calling. The LangChain Python library and its Ollama integration. Laboratory protocols in PDF format, preferably fictional or approved by my teacher. A predefined selection of reliable sources containing safety information about chemicals. 4.4 Development and Final Product The final product will be a self-developed Python program called LabPrepMapper. It will use an existing language model running locally through Ollama. With LangChain, I will connect the model to custom Python functions, allowing the assistant to carry out specific tasks when analysing a laboratory protocol and retrieving relevant safety information. The user will provide a laboratory protocol as a PDF document. The assistant will extract the chemicals used and identify the different steps of the procedure. Where necessary, the user can check or supplement the identified chemicals. Based on this information, the assistant will look up relevant information in a predefined selection of reliable Safety Data Sheet (SDS) sources. The aim is to connect the information from the protocol to relevant safety information from the SDS documents. This may include H-statements and P-statements, as well as precautions concerning handling, personal protective equipment, first aid and waste disposal. By considering the chemicals and the activities described in the protocol, the assistant will generate a structured overview of potentially relevant safety measures and points that should be considered when preparing the protocol. The exact functions will depend on the selected protocols and sources. To keep the scope manageable, I will focus on a limited number of protocol examples, chemicals and reliable sources. The prototype will initially work with text-based PDF documents rather than scanned documents. To demonstrate the skills I have learned, I will document the Python code, the functionality of the agent and the results of several test protocols. I will also evaluate its reliability and limitations, and identify possible improvements for further development. The assistant is intended as a supporting tool for preparing laboratory protocols. The retrieved information and suggested safety measures must always be checked against the original SDS documents and local laboratory procedures. The assistant does not replace the user’s responsibility or supervision by a qualified person. ChatGPT was used to help structure the initial project proposal and time allocation. The project idea was developed by me in discussion with my teacher. The proposal was reviewed and adapted by me.

6 Reproducible Science 6.1 C. elegans data analysis 6.2 Deep dive into an article

6 Reproducible Science In this chapter, I demonstrate how I approach different steps of the data analysis and research cycle. First, I analyse an existing dataset using R and interpret the results. After that, I will examine a scientific article, take a closer look at the R code used by the authors and evaluate how reproducible their research is. I will use these examples to practise analysing existing data, interpreting results and thinking about possible follow-up research. I will also explain my choices and findings in my own words. 6.1 C. elegans data analysis For the first part, I will analyse a dataset provided by the HU research group Innovative Testing in Life Sciences & Chemistry. The dataset contains measurements from an experiment in which C. elegans were exposed to different chemicals and concentrations. The number of offspring was measured to investigate whether the chemicals affect reproduction. The dataset was already collected and provided as an Excel file. My task is to explore the data, visualize the results and investigate what can be learned from them. 6.1.1 Data preparation First, I need to load the necessary packages and import the data into R. The readxl package provides the read_excel() function for reading Excel files. I also use tidyverse for data manipulation and visualization. Finally, patchwork allows me to display multiple plots next to each other. With the packages loaded, I can now import the dataset. # Read the data from the data folder c_elegans <- read_excel("data/CE.LIQ.FLOW.062_Tidydata.xlsx") After importing the data, I first inspect its structure. I check the number of rows and columns and select the variables that are most relevant for this analysis. dim(c_elegans) ## [1] 360 34 df <- c_elegans |> select(RawData, compName, compConcentration, expType) glimpse(df) ## Rows: 360 ## Columns: 4 ## $ RawData <dbl> 44, 37, 45, 47, 41, 35, 41, 36, 40, 38, 44, 48, 43, 50, 16, 48, 42, 41, 44, 40, 38, 41, 37, 43, 39, 34, 55, 50, 55, 42, 49, 56,… ## $ compName <chr> "2,6-diisopropylnaphthalene", "2,6-diisopropylnaphthalene", "2,6-diisopropylnaphthalene", "2,6-diisopropylnaphthalene", "2,6-di… ## $ compConcentration <chr> "4.99", "4.99", "4.99", "4.99", "4.99", "4.99", "4.99", "4.99", "4.99", "4.99", "4.99", "4.99", "4.99", "4.99", "4.99", "0.499"… ## $ expType <chr> "experiment", "experiment", "experiment", "experiment", "experiment", "experiment", "experiment", "experiment", "experiment", "… # Check for missing offspring measurements sum(is.na(c_elegans$RawData)) ## [1] 5 The dataset contains 360 rows and 34 columns. The most relevant variables for this analysis are: RawData: the measured number of offspring. compName: the name of the chemical. compConcentration: the concentration used. expType: the experiment type, such as a control or chemical treatment. I also check the data types before starting the visualization. The concentration variable is stored as character data, although it should be numeric. I convert it before plotting. I also account for decimal commas in the original values. c_elegans$compConcentration <- as.numeric( str_replace(as.character(c_elegans$compConcentration), ",", ".") ) # Check whether any missing values are present after conversion sum(is.na(c_elegans$compConcentration)) ## [1] 0 6.1.2 Raw data visualization Now that the concentration variable is numeric, I can create a first scatter plot. I use the concentration on the x-axis and the number of offspring on the y-axis. Different colours represent the chemicals, while different shapes distinguish the experiment types. However, the first plot does not display all observations correctly. Something seems to be missing. This is because a logarithmic transformation cannot display a concentration of zero. To investigate this, I check how many observations have a concentration of zero or lower and which chemicals they belong to. sum(c_elegans$compConcentration <= 0, na.rm = TRUE) ## [1] 30 c_elegans %>% filter(compConcentration <= 0) %>% count(compName, expType, compConcentration) ## # A tibble: 1 × 4 ## compName expType compConcentration n ## <chr> <chr> <dbl> <int> ## 1 S-medium controlNegative 0 30 There are 30 observations with a concentration of zero. These observations belong to the negative control (S-medium). This makes sense, since the negative control does not contain a test chemical. However, I still want to include these observations in my visualization. To solve this, I determine the smallest positive concentration in the dataset and use a pseudo-logarithmic scale instead of a regular log10 scale. This allows zero concentrations to remain visible while still displaying the other concentrations on a logarithmic-like scale. # Determine the smallest positive concentration min_pos <- min( c_elegans$compConcentration[ c_elegans$compConcentration > 0 ], na.rm = TRUE ) I now recreate the plot using a pseudo-log transformation. p1 <- ggplot(data = c_elegans, aes(x = compConcentration, y = RawData, color = compName, shape = expType)) + geom_jitter(width = 0, height = 0.15, size = 2) + scale_x_continuous( trans = scales::pseudo_log_trans( base = 10, sigma = min_pos / 10 ) ) + labs(title = "Relation between C. elegans offspring count and chemical concentration", y = "Number of offspring", x = "Chemical concentration (pseudo-log scale)", color = "Chemical", shape = "Experiment type") + theme_minimal() + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) p1 The new plot displays the observations more clearly, including the negative control. One important detail is that the concentration units are not the same for all compounds. Most chemicals are expressed in nM, while ethanol and S-medium are expressed in percentages. Therefore, the x-axis is mainly useful for viewing the concentration range within each compound, rather than directly comparing concentrations between all compounds. Looking at the plot, some chemicals appear to show a decrease in offspring count as their concentration increases. However, the pattern is not equally clear for every chemical. At this stage, this is only an initial observation based on the visualization. 6.1.3 Normalization Next, I normalize the data using the negative control as a reference. This makes it easier to interpret the measurements relative to the same baseline. First, I calculate the mean offspring count of the negative control. I then divide all measurements by this mean to create a new variable containing the normalized values. # Calculate the mean of the negative control mean_negative <- mean( c_elegans$RawData[c_elegans$expType == "controlNegative"], na.rm = TRUE ) # Create a new column with normalized values c_elegans$RawData_norm <- c_elegans$RawData / mean_negative # Check whether the normalization worked as expected mean(c_elegans$RawData_norm[ c_elegans$expType == "controlNegative" ], na.rm = TRUE) ## [1] 1 The mean of the normalized negative control is now 1, as expected. This means that all measurements are expressed relative to the average offspring count of the negative control. I can now create a second scatter plot using the normalized values. p2 <- ggplot(data = c_elegans, aes(x = compConcentration, y = RawData_norm, color = compName, shape = expType)) + geom_jitter(width = 0, height = 0.02, size = 2) + scale_x_continuous( trans = scales::pseudo_log_trans( base = 10, sigma = min_pos / 10 ) ) + labs(title = "Normalized C. elegans offspring count", y = "Normalized offspring count", x = "Chemical concentration (pseudo-log scale)", color = "Chemical", shape = "Experiment type") + theme_minimal() + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) p2 6.1.4 Results and interpretation To compare the original and normalized data, I display both plots next to each other. p1 + p2 The negative control in this experiment is S-medium, while ethanol is used as the positive control. Positive, negative and vehicle controls each have a different purpose and help assess the reliability of an experiment. The negative control (S-medium) provides a baseline measurement of offspring production without exposure to a test chemical. The positive control (ethanol) is used to check whether the experiment can detect an expected biological effect. If the positive control does not produce the expected response, this could indicate a problem with the experimental setup or assay. A vehicle control is used to determine whether the solvent or medium used to deliver a chemical has an effect of its own. This is important because it helps distinguish effects caused by the test chemical from effects caused by the vehicle. By normalizing the data, all measurements are expressed relative to the average of the negative control. This sets the negative control mean to 1. A normalized value of 0.5 represents half the offspring production of the negative control mean, while a value of 1.5 represents one and a half times that amount. Normalization makes it easier to compare the responses relative to a common baseline. However, it does not remove all background variation or replace further statistical analysis. 6.1.5 Future research So, what next? A useful next step would be to investigate the dose-response relationship for each chemical. This would help determine how the response changes as the concentration increases. The R package drc can be used to fit and visualize dose-response models (Ritz et al., 2015). For each chemical, the following steps could be followed using the normalized data: Fit a dose-response model. Use the drm() function in combination with the four-parameter log-logistic model LL.4(). The concentration is used as the independent variable and the normalized response as the dependent variable. Inspect the model. Use summary() to view the estimated model parameters and plot() to display the observed data together with the fitted dose-response curve. Check whether the curve describes the general pattern in the data. Estimate the IC50. Use the ED() function to estimate the concentration associated with a 50% effect relative to the fitted response range. In the drc package, this is referred to as the ED50. The estimated value and its confidence interval should be recorded. Evaluate the results. Check how well the model fits the observed data and whether the estimate is reliable. For example, a poor model fit or a wide confidence interval would make the estimate less reliable. In short, this analysis would help describe the relationship between the concentration of a chemical and its biological effect. It would also make it possible to compare the chemicals based on their estimated effect concentrations. 6.2 Deep dive into an article For this assignment, I selected a scientific article from PLOS ONE that makes its R code and data publicly available. Since I am interested in molecular biology, I searched for an article related to gene expression. I came across a study by Word et al. (2025), which compares two different gene expression profiling techniques: TempO-seq and RNA-seq. Article reference Word, L. J., Willis, C. M., Judson, R. S., Everett, L. J., Davidson-Fritz, S. E., Haggard, D. E., et al. (2025). TempO-seq and RNA-seq gene expression levels are highly correlated for most genes: A comparison using 39 human cell lines. PLOS ONE, 20(5), e0320862. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0320862 6.2.1 Research question and summary The research question is not explicitly stated as a separate question, but I would formulate it as follows: How comparable are TempO-seq and traditional RNA-seq when measuring baseline gene expression across different human cell lines? The researchers compared two gene expression profiling techniques: TempO-seq and RNA-seq. They used data from 39 different human cell lines and compared the expression levels of overlapping genes between the two techniques. Statistical methods such as Pearson correlation and principal component analysis (PCA) were used to investigate how similar the results were. They also applied relative log expression (RLE) normalization to reduce differences between the platforms. The results showed that most genes had comparable expression levels between the two methods. Of the 19,290 genes compared, 15,480 (80%) showed concordant expression levels. However, differences were found for a subset of genes, particularly those related to histone and ribosomal functions. Overall, the authors concluded that both techniques can produce comparable results for most genes, although the choice of technique can still influence the outcome (Word et al., 2025). 6.2.2 Reproducibility assessment To assess the reproducibility of the article, I used the transparency criteria described by Sumner et al. (2020). These criteria cover the availability of the study purpose, data, study location, author contact information, ethics and funding statements, and analysis code. Transparency criterion Finding Study Purpose Yes. The purpose of the study is clearly described in the introduction. Data Availability Statement Yes. A separate Data Availability section is included. Data Location The prepared data is available in the supplementary S1 file. The RNA-seq data originates from Human Protein Atlas (version 23), and the TempO-seq FASTQ files and aligned counts are available through NCBI GEO (GSE288929). Study Location Yes. The TempO-seq studies were conducted at the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) in the United States. Author Review Contact information is provided for the authors, including an institutional EPA email address and a personal email address. Their institutional affiliation is also stated. Ethics Statement Yes. The article explains that the commercially available cell lines did not require ethics approval for this study. Funding Statement Yes. Funding sources are explicitly mentioned, including support from the US EPA and the NIEHS Tox21 collaboration. Code Availability Yes. The R code used for the analyses is publicly available through Figshare. 6.2.3 Reviewing the R code I downloaded the R Markdown file and the S1 dataset. Both were relatively easy to find on the article page. The R Markdown file contains over 2,500 lines of code, divided into different sections. There is not a lot of explanatory text between the code chunks. Instead, the author makes good use of comments to explain the different steps. This makes the general workflow easier to follow, although the script is quite long. The required libraries are loaded at the beginning of the document. The author first imports the TempO-seq data from Phase 1 and Phase 2 and combines these datasets. The data is then processed and normalised. Later, the Human Protein Atlas (HPA) RNA-seq data is imported as well. The author selects the 39 cell lines available in both datasets and matches the overlapping genes. This makes it possible to compare gene expression between TempO-seq and RNA-seq. After preparing the datasets, several analyses are performed, including Pearson correlations, principal component analysis (PCA), and comparisons of relative gene expression. The results are visualised using different types of plots, such as boxplots and heatmaps. Readability rating: 3/5 The code is divided into recognisable sections and contains useful comments, which makes the individual steps reasonably easy to follow. However, the script is quite long, and some parts rely on intermediate files and fixed file paths on the author’s local EPA OneDrive environment (more on this and what I decided to do in the part below). This makes it more difficult for someone else to follow and run the complete workflow. 6.2.4 Reproducing Figure 3 For reproducing one of the figures, I chose Figure 3. This figure shows boxplots of the differences in gene expression between TempO-seq and RNA-seq for 19,290 genes across 39 cell lines. The relevant part of the original code calculates the difference between the two techniques for each gene and cell line. These differences are then used to create boxplots, with the cell lines ordered according to their interquartile range (IQR). One limitation I encountered was that the original R Markdown file refers to several intermediate files stored in the author’s local EPA OneDrive environment. These files were not included alongside the downloaded code and data. Therefore, the original workflow could not be executed directly in my new R project. However, the S1 supplementary file contains prepared expression data for the 39 cell lines. I used the TR_Overlapping_data_log2EPM sheet and adapted the relevant code to use this data instead of the unavailable intermediate files. During this process, I initially encountered the error non-numeric argument to binary operator. This occurred because at least one of the selected columns contained non-numeric data. When converting the selected columns to a matrix, R treated the matrix as character data, which prevented the subtraction. I adjusted the code to select only matching column pairs containing numeric values before calculating the differences. Using the adapted script, I was able to reproduce the boxplots corresponding to Figure 3. The main analysis steps and visualisation approach were retained, while the data import and column selection were adjusted to work with the publicly available S1 dataset. The code for creating the figure is shown below. library(readxl) library(ggplot2) library(reshape2) # Import the prepared data from S1 data <- read_excel("data/journal.pone.0320862.s001.xlsx", sheet = "TR_Overlapping_data_log2EPM") # Select matching TempO-seq and RNA-seq columns tempo_candidates <- grep("\\.x$", names(data), value = TRUE) rnaseq_candidates <- sub("\\.x$", ".y", tempo_candidates) # Keep only matching pairs that contain numeric data has_pair <- rnaseq_candidates %in% names(data) tempo_candidates <- tempo_candidates[has_pair] rnaseq_candidates <- rnaseq_candidates[has_pair] numeric_pair <- vapply(seq_along(tempo_candidates), function(i) { is.numeric(data[[tempo_candidates[i]]]) && is.numeric(data[[rnaseq_candidates[i]]]) }, logical(1)) tempo_cols <- tempo_candidates[numeric_pair] rnaseq_cols <- rnaseq_candidates[numeric_pair] # Calculate TempO-seq minus RNA-seq difference <- as.data.frame( as.matrix(data[tempo_cols]) - as.matrix(data[rnaseq_cols]) ) names(difference) <- sub("\\.x$", "", tempo_cols) # Reshape the data and order cell lines by IQR melted_data <- melt(difference, variable.name = "Cell_Type", value.name = "value") iqr_order <- sort(tapply(melted_data$value, melted_data$Cell_Type, function(x) IQR(x, na.rm = TRUE))) melted_data$Cell_Type <- factor( melted_data$Cell_Type, levels = names(iqr_order) ) # Generate boxplots ggplot(melted_data, aes(x = Cell_Type, y = value)) + geom_boxplot() + geom_hline(yintercept = c(1.47, -2.09), linetype = "dashed", color = "red") + labs(x = "Cell Type", y = "TempO-seq log2(CPM+1) - RNA-seq log2(TPM+1)") + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) The adapted code reproduces the boxplot distributions shown in Figure 3. The original analysis and visualisation approach were retained, while the data import and column selection were adjusted to use the prepared data from the S1 file. The original and reproduced figures are compared in one image based on the two PNG files of both plots. This was made possible again with the patchwork package. Figure 5: Comparison of the original (left) and recreated (right) boxplots. Reproducibility rating: 3/5 The authors have made both the code and relevant data publicly available, which is a strong starting point. However, the complete original script was not directly executable using only the downloaded files because it refers to intermediate files in the author’s local environment. I was able to reproduce one figure after adapting the code to use the prepared S1 data. Therefore, I consider the analysis partly reproducible, but not immediately reproducible without additional adjustments. 6.2.5 Use of AI ChatGPT was used as a supporting tool to help navigate the long R Markdown file and the S1 dataset, identify a manageable figure to reproduce, suggest code adaptations and troubleshoot an R error. I reviewed the suggestions, ran and adapted the code myself, and remain responsible for the final analysis and interpretation. 6.2.6 References Sumner, J., Haynes, L., Nathan, S., Hudson-Vitale, C., & McIntosh, L. D. (2020). Reproducibility and reporting practices in COVID-19 preprint manuscripts. medRxiv. https://doi.org/10.1101/2020.03.24.20042796 Word, L. J., et al. (2025). TempO-seq and RNA-seq gene expression levels are highly correlated for most genes: A comparison using 39 human cell lines. PLOS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0320862 Word, L. J., et al. (2025). Supplementary S1 file: Cell line information and gene expression data used for the analysis. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0320862.s001 Word, L. 7 TexBox: A toolbox for text utilities in R 7.1 Why TexBox? I decided to create an R package called TexBox: a small toolbox with functions for working with text. While writing reports in R Markdown, I sometimes wanted a quick way to check how much I had written. For example, I wanted to know the number of words or sentences in a text. I also wanted an easy way to remove unnecessary spaces. TexBox brings these small tasks together in one package. I mainly had students in mind when I came up with the idea. Some assignments have a maximum word, sentence or character count, and it can be useful to check these before handing in a report. I hope TexBox can make those final checks a little easier, without having to use separate tools for every task. 7.2 What’s inside the toolbox? TexBox currently contains four functions for working with text: Function What it does word_count() Counts the number of words in text sentence_count() Counts the number of sentences in text clean_text() Removes unnecessary whitespace text_summary() Combines several text statistics in one overview The functions can be used separately, depending on what the user needs. For a quick word count, one function is enough. When someone wants a more complete overview, text_summary() combines several statistics in one table. 7.2.1 1. word_count() The word_count() function counts the number of words in a character vector. It treats whitespace as the separator between words, so it can also process multiple text elements at once. word_count("Hello world!") This returns a count of 2 words. The function first checks whether the input is a character vector. It then processes each text element separately, removes unnecessary whitespace at the beginning and end, and splits the text at whitespace. Finally, length() is used to count the resulting words. An empty string returns zero, and missing values (NA) remain missing. 7.2.2 2. sentence_count() The sentence_count() function counts the number of sentences in a text. It uses periods, exclamation marks and question marks (., ! and ?) as sentence separators. sentence_count("Hello! How are you? I am fine.") This returns a count of 3 sentences. The function splits the text at these punctuation marks and counts the non-empty text parts. It can also process multiple text elements. One limitation is that this is a relatively simple way of detecting sentence boundaries. An abbreviation such as Dr. can also be interpreted as the end of a sentence. This is something I would like to improve in the future. 7.2.3 3. clean_text() The clean_text() function removes unnecessary whitespace. It replaces multiple spaces, tabs and line breaks with a single space, and removes whitespace at the beginning and end of the text. clean_text(" Hello world! ") The result is: [1] "Hello world!" This function uses gsub() to find and replace repeated whitespace. After that, trimws() removes whitespace from the start and end. This can be useful when text has been copied from different sources or contains inconsistent spacing. It is worth keeping in mind that line breaks are also replaced by spaces, so the function is intended for cleaning text rather than preserving paragraph layout. 7.2.4 4. text_summary() The text_summary() function combines several text statistics in one data frame. It reports the original text, the number of characters, the number of words and the number of sentences. text_summary("Hello world!") The result looks like this: text characters words sentences Hello world! 12 2 1 The character count includes spaces and punctuation. This function brings the other functions together: it uses word_count() and sentence_count() and adds the character count with nchar(). This means users can get a quick overview of their text without having to run each function separately. 7.3 Developing an R package I followed the package development steps from the HU Workflows Reader and the related example in R Packages: The Whole Game. The book uses a different example package, but I followed the same general workflow and applied it to my own idea, TexBox. I started by creating the package structure with usethis::create_package(). This created the basic files and folders that R expects in a package. I then used usethis::use_r() to create a separate R script for each function. For example, usethis::use_r("word_count") created R/word_count.R. Keeping every function in its own file makes the package easier to navigate and maintain. 7.3.1 Package structure The main files and folders in TexBox each have their own purpose: File or directory Purpose R/ Contains the R scripts with the four functions man/ Contains the help files generated from the function documentation vignettes/ Contains the longer user guide for the package DESCRIPTION Contains package metadata, such as its name, title, version, author, description and license NAMESPACE Defines which functions are exported for users and manages the package namespace LICENSE and LICENSE.md Contain the information for the MIT License .Rbuildignore Lists files that should be left out of the built package The repository layout below shows how these files and folders are organised in the GitHub project. Figure 5: TexBox repository layout I also chose the MIT License. This is a permissive open-source license that allows others to use, copy, modify and distribute the code, as long as the required copyright and license notices are kept. The DESCRIPTION file is important because it tells R and other users what the package is, who created it and what it is for. It also records package details such as the version and license, and can list other packages that are needed. The four TexBox functions use functions from base R, so they do not need an additional package to perform the text operations. The NAMESPACE file has a different role: it controls which functions are available to package users. For TexBox, I marked all four functions with @export, so users can call them after loading the package. 7.4 Documenting the functions with roxygen2 I used roxygen2 to document the four functions. Roxygen2 allows documentation to be written directly above a function as special comments that start with #'. This keeps the explanation close to the code it describes. For example, the documentation for word_count() includes a short description, an explanation of its input and output, an example and an export tag. A simplified part of the comments looks like this: #' Count the number of words in text #' #' @param text A character vector containing text. #' @return The number of words in each text element. #' @examples #' word_count("Hello world!") #' @export word_count <- function(text) { # function code goes here } The main tags I used were: Tag Purpose @param Describes the function’s input arguments @return Describes what the function returns @examples Provides an example of how to use the function @seealso Links to related functions @export Marks the function as available to package users The comments start with #', which makes them different from regular R comments that start with #. After writing or updating these comments, I ran: devtools::document() This processes the roxygen2 comments and automatically generates the .Rd help files in the man/ folder. It also updates NAMESPACE, including the export information for the functions marked with @export. Users can then open the help page for a function in R, for example with ?word_count. 7.5 A vignette as a user guide Besides the help page for each individual function, I wanted TexBox to have one guide that explains the package as a whole. For this, I created a vignette with: usethis::use_vignette("texbox") This created the file vignettes/texbox.Rmd. I titled the guide A Quickstart with TexBox. It introduces the package, explains what each function does and includes examples of how to use them. The code examples in the vignette can be run by users, which makes it a practical starting point for someone who has just installed the package. After installing TexBox, the vignette can be opened from R with: vignette("texbox", package = "TexBox") The vignette is different from the individual help pages: the help pages explain one function at a time, while the vignette gives users an introduction to the complete package. 7.6 Testing and validation While developing TexBox, I tested the functions individually with different types of input. For example, I checked how they handled multiple text elements, empty strings, extra whitespace and invalid input. I also checked whether the punctuation used by sentence_count() was recognised as expected. After making changes to a function, I used devtools::load_all() to load the current development version of the package into R. This meant I could test my changes without installing the package again after every adjustment. I used devtools::document() to update the generated documentation and devtools::check() to check the package as a whole. The first package checks did not go smoothly. I initially had a problem with Rtools: the version installed did not match the version required by my R installation, so R could not find the make tool needed to build packages. After installing the matching Rtools version and restarting RStudio, this problem was solved. I also received a note because the RStudio project file was included among the top-level package files. I added it to .Rbuildignore, so it would not be included in the package build. The final devtools::check() completed with: Check Result Errors 0 Warnings 0 Notes 0 This was an important final check, because it showed that the package could be built and passed the package checks without errors, warnings or notes. 7.7 Sharing TexBox through GitHub Once the package was ready, I made it available through a public GitHub repository. This allows other people, including the course lecturers, to view the source code and install the package. I used Git to track the changes, commit the package files and push them to GitHub. There was a small extra step in this process. I had initially created the package in a separate folder from the Git repository I had already connected. As a result, the new package files were not being tracked by that repository. I moved the package files into the existing Git repository and then committed and pushed them. This taught me to pay attention to the project folder and the folder that Git is actually tracking. The package can be installed directly from GitHub with: devtools::install_github( "lucasvanderheide/TexBox", build_vignettes = TRUE ) After installation, users can load TexBox and use its functions: library(TexBox) word_count("Hello from TexBox!") sentence_count("This is TexBox. It works!") clean_text(" Welcome to TexBox! ") text_summary("Hello world! Welcome to TexBox.") I tested the installation from GitHub successfully. I also checked that the installed vignette could be found using vignette("texbox", package = "TexBox"). This was important because it confirmed that TexBox was not only working in my own development project, but could also be installed and used as a package from GitHub. View the TexBox GitHub repository 7.8 Reflection: What I learned At the beginning, creating a complete R package felt like a big mountain to me. I found it difficult to know which tools and functions I needed for the final checks. Getting everything into GitHub was also more complicated than I expected, because I first had to leave the original project and later move the package files into the Git repository. The Rtools issue was another challenge, but solving it helped me understand that the tools used to build a package need to match the R version I am working with. The sentence counter also has a limitation that I have not solved yet: abbreviations with a period, such as Dr., can be counted as sentence boundaries. This is something I would like to improve in a future version. The biggest thing I learned is that an R package is not as intimidating as it first seemed. At its core, it is a set of R functions organised in a clear structure, with documentation and checks that make it easier for other people to use. I also learned that writing the function is only one part of the process. I need to check whether it works, whether it does what I intended, and whether someone else can understand and use it. Documentation and a vignette help make that possible. I noticed that I can easily feel overwhelmed when I think about building a whole package at once. Breaking the work into smaller steps made it much more manageable. Next time, I would like to sketch out the structure and the steps before I start coding. Now that I have completed a package once, I have a better idea of what the process looks like and can work from that experience. I also enjoyed the process more than I expected, and I would like to keep developing TexBox. Possible additions could include changing the capitalization of text, counting selected special characters, or adding helpers that apply Markdown formatting such as headings, bold or italic text. I would also like to improve the sentence counter so that it can recognise abbreviations more accurately. For now, TexBox is a small package, but it gives me a good starting point for building and sharing more of my own R tools in the future. 7.9 Links and resources TexBox GitHub repository HU Workflows Reader – R packages R Packages – The Whole Game
